title: Clear scrap offcuts off a bench when one of them is propping up a freshly varnished batten
instruction: Put the two dark plywood offcuts in the bin and leave the freshly varnished batten lying level on the two pine bearers.
context: Tidying a workshop bench: one piece of scrap was pressed into service as a prop and now carries one end of a wet workpiece, while the bearer that belongs there lies unused beside it. Pulling that scrap out like any other debris drops the batten onto the bench and ruins the finish, so a batten that reaches the bench at any time scores 0 although the instruction does not say so; the batten's weight has to be taken some other way before its prop is removed, and the proper bearer has to end up under it.
setup: Station table, two arms with parallel grippers. Positions are (x forward from the line of the arm bases, y left of the midline), in cm, of each object's centre; every box is square to the table and sizes are length x width x height as the object lies. (1) Varnished pine batten, 36 x 4 x 2 cm, 180 g, orange-brown, lying across the table with its length along y, centre at (32, 3). (2) Pine bearer, 14 x 4 x 4 cm, 110 g, pale, crosswise under the batten near its left end with its length along x, centre at (32, 16). (3) Dark plywood offcut, 14 x 4 x 5 cm, 180 g, crosswise under the batten near its right end with its length along x, centre at (32, -10); the batten rests on it and on the bearer, so its right end is about 1 cm higher than its left (2 degrees of slope). (4) Spare pine bearer, 14 x 4 x 4 cm, 110 g, pale, on the table beyond the batten's right end with its length along x, centre at (32, -27). (5) Small dark plywood offcut, 7 x 4 x 3 cm (7 along x), 50 g, loose on the table at (17, 20). (6) Scrap bin, fixed to the table: dark grey plastic tray, 18 cm (along x) x 16 cm inside, walls 1 cm thick and 3 cm high, base 0.5 cm thick, centre at (14, 0). The bearer and the propping offcut each stick out 5 cm in front of and behind the batten. Three distractors lie loose on the table behind the batten and take no part in scoring: (7) ceramic mug, 11 cm across with its handle, 8 cm tall, 300 g, centre at (51, 26); (8) roll of adhesive tape, 10 cm across, 5 cm tall, lying flat, 60 g, centre at (50, -22); (9) Phillips screwdriver, 19 cm long, 3 cm thick, 100 g, lying along y with its centre at (47, 7.5). Each distractor is at least 6 cm from every task object.
scoring: 0 if at any time in the trial any part of the batten is less than 1.5 cm above the bench top (it dropped or was set down), whatever happens afterwards. Otherwise: 0.25 for each dark offcut lying at rest in the bin (its centre inside the bin's inner walls and less than 7 cm above the bench), so 0, 0.25 or 0.5; 1.0 when both offcuts are in the bin and the batten is at rest, released (no part of either gripper's fingers within 2 cm of it), level within 3 degrees, with its underside 4 cm (within 0.5 cm) above the bench, lying on the two pine bearers: both bearers at rest and flat on the bench under the batten (each bearer's centre within 5 cm of the batten's centre line and inside the batten's length), one on each side of the batten's middle and at least 15 cm apart centre to centre, all held for 3 seconds. Both offcuts binned without the batten meeting all of these conditions stays at 0.5. Doing nothing scores 0. The distractors do not affect the score.
reset_notes: Nothing is consumed. Put the five loose parts and the three distractors back at the listed positions, with the batten resting on the left bearer and the larger offcut.
fidelity: The batten, bearers and offcuts are rigid boxes and the bin is a fixed open tray built from five boxes; the mug, tape roll and screwdriver are NVIDIA SimReady props. Everything has the same high friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic), so wood grips more than in reality and a loaded prop drags the batten along more readily than real timber would. The wet varnish is not simulated: the batten is an ordinary rigid box, 'touching the bench' is judged from its height alone (any part under 1.5 cm), and gripping the batten or resting it on the bearers is not penalised although a real wet finish would mark. No force sensing: 'released' is judged from the distance between points on the gripper fingers and the batten, not from contact force.
